summary: Arabic subject pronouns mark person, number and — in the 2nd and 3rd person — gender: أَنَا I, أَنْتَ you (a man), أَنْتِ you (a woman), هُوَ he, هِيَ she, نَحْنُ we, أَنْتُمْ you (men or a mixed group), أَنْتُنَّ you (women), هُمْ they (men or mixed), هُنَّ they (women). Exactly two people have dual pronouns: أَنْتُمَا (you two) and هُمَا (they two). There is no “it”: a thing is هُوَ or هِيَ by its gender, and every plural of things is هِيَ. Before a verb the pronoun is usually left out, because the verb ending shows the person; in a sentence without a verb it is needed: أَنَا طَالِبٌ.

head: one (singular)
several (plural)
two (dual)
rows: هُوَ huwa — he; it (a masculine thing)
هِيَ hiya — she; it (a feminine thing; things in the plural)
blocks.caption: The dual pronouns come with the dual of nouns and verbs (lesson 5); here they are for recognition.

blocks.title: No “it”.
blocks.text: الْبَابُ؟ هُوَ هُنَا (the door? it is here) — الْغُرْفَةُ؟ هِيَ هُنَاكَ (the room? it is there) — الْكُتُبُ؟ هِيَ هُنَا (the books? they are here): a plural of things is هِيَ.

blocks.title: Mixed groups are masculine.
blocks.text: One man among many women is enough for أَنْتُمْ and هُمْ; only an all-female group is أَنْتُنَّ / هُنَّ.

items.title: With a verb
points: the ending already shows the person: كُنْتُ = I was, كَانَتْ = she was
the pronoun adds emphasis or contrast: أَنَا كُنْتُ طَالِبًا = it was I who was a student

items.title: Without a verb
points: the pronoun is the subject and cannot be dropped
أَنَا طَالِبٌ = I am a student; هِيَ مُعَلِّمَةٌ = she is a teacher

blocks.text: There is no polite “you”: أَنْتَ / أَنْتِ is said to everyone, even to strangers and to the old. Respect comes from titles and formulas: يَا أُسْتَاذُ (sir), حَضْرَتُكَ (your presence).

notes.text: German Sie has no Arabic counterpart: to a stranger you still say أَنْتَ or أَنْتِ, and add a title (يَا أُسْتَاذُ).
No вы for one person: أَنْتُمْ is only for several people; politeness comes from titles and formulas.
No polite εσείς: أَنْتُمْ means several people, never one person addressed politely.
No vous de politesse: one person is always أَنْتَ / أَنْتِ.
No siz for one person: أَنْتُمْ is plural only; respect is shown with titles such as حَضْرَتُكَ.

askYourself: Who is it: me, the person I speak to, or someone else?
A man or a woman (2nd and 3rd person)? A mixed group counts as masculine.
Is it a thing? → هُوَ or هِيَ by the noun’s gender; a plural of things → هِيَ.
Is there a verb? → the pronoun may be dropped; no verb → keep it.

traps: أَنْتَ and أَنْتِ look the same without vowels (انت): pronounce the last vowel clearly.
*الْكُتُبُ؟ هُمْ هُنَا is wrong: things in the plural are هِيَ.
هُوَ / هِيَ also mean “it”; there is no separate word.
For exactly two people careful MSA uses أَنْتُمَا / هُمَا, not أَنْتُمْ / هُمْ.

quiz.why: أَنْتِ (-ti) for one woman; أَنْتُنَّ for several women.

quiz.q: “They” for five women and one man:

quiz.why: Plurals of things take the feminine singular.
The dual pronoun is for two.
نَحْنُ is for men, women, two or more.

seeAlso.note: Hebrew has the same Semitic set — אַתָּה / אַתְּ, אַתֶּם / אַתֶּן, הֵם / הֵן; אֲנִי ↔ أَنَا, אֲנַחְנוּ ↔ نَحْنُ — but no dual pronouns.
German has a polite Sie and a neuter es; Arabic has neither and marks the listener’s gender instead (أَنْتَ / أَنْتِ).
Chinese 他 / 她 / 它 are all pronounced tā — the gender is only in the writing; the plural adds 们.
German also calls things by their gender — der Tisch → er, die Tür → sie — just like Arabic هُوَ / هِيَ; only German has es for neuters.

notes.text: Greek also drops the pronoun because the verb ending shows the person (τρώω), and has gender in the 3rd person (αυτός / αυτή / αυτό). Arabic also marks the gender of “you” (أَنْتَ / أَنْتِ) and has no neuter: a thing is هُوَ or هِيَ.
Russian он / она / оно also name things by their gender; Arabic has no neuter, so a thing is هُوَ or هِيَ. Russian keeps я with a verb (я ем), Arabic usually drops it (آكُلُ).

As in Spanish, the pronoun is dropped before a verb (como → آكُلُ), and “they” and “you (plural)” have masculine and feminine forms (ellos / ellas ≈ هُمْ / هُنَّ, vosotros / vosotras ≈ أَنْتُمْ / أَنْتُنَّ). New: the singular “you” also has gender, and there are dual pronouns.

English shows gender only in he / she / it; Arabic shows it in “you” (أَنْتَ to a man, أَنْتِ to a woman) and in “they” too, has no “it” (a thing is هُوَ or هِيَ), and usually leaves the pronoun out before a verb.
French il / elle also name things by their gender (la table → elle), and ils / elles split “they” like هُمْ / هُنَّ; Arabic adds the gender of “you”.
German er / sie name things by gender too (der Tisch → er), but Arabic has no neuter es: every thing is هُوَ or هِيَ.
Hindi वह covers he, she and it, and chooses “you” by respect (तू, तुम, आप); Arabic chooses “you” by the listener’s gender and number, never by respect.

Persian او is both he and she, and شما is the polite “you”; Arabic splits “you” and “they” by gender and has no polite pronoun. Like Persian, it drops the pronoun because the verb ending shows the person.
Marathi has gender in the 3rd person (तो / ती / ते) and two words for “we” (आम्ही, आपण); Arabic has one نَحْنُ but adds gender to “you” (أَنْتَ / أَنْتِ).
Hebrew has the same Semitic set, gender in “you” and “they” included (אַתָּה / אַתְּ, הֵם / הֵן) — but no dual pronouns.
Turkish o is he, she and it; Arabic must choose هُوَ or هِيَ, and splits “you” and “they” by gender too. Like Turkish, it leaves the pronoun out when the verb ending shows the person.
Japanese leaves pronouns out and picks them by politeness; Arabic has one small set chosen by person, number and gender, and needs the pronoun in a sentence without a verb (أَنَا طَالِبٌ).
Korean avoids “you” and uses titles or names; Arabic says أَنْتَ / أَنْتِ to anyone — respect comes from titles and formulas, not from another pronoun.
Finnish hän is both he and she; Arabic must choose هُوَ or هِيَ — also for things, since there is no “it”. Like Finnish, it drops the pronoun before a verb.
Hungarian ő is both he and she, and polite ön / maga takes 3rd-person verbs; Arabic has gendered pronouns and no polite form.
Swahili yeye is both he and she, and things are referred to by their noun class; Arabic uses هُوَ or هِيَ by sex-based gender, for people and things alike.
Luganda ye is both he and she; Arabic splits هُوَ / هِيَ, and also أَنْتَ / أَنْتِ and هُمْ / هُنَّ.
Chinese 他 / 她 / 它 all sound tā; Arabic gender is heard: huwa / hiya, ʾanta / ʾanti. Arabic has one “we”, نَحْنُ, for both 我们 and 咱们.
Vietnamese uses kinship words as pronouns (anh, chị, em, ông, bà), chosen by age and respect; Arabic has one fixed set chosen by person, number and gender, and one “we” for chúng ta and chúng tôi.
Inuktitut also has dual pronouns and person endings (uvaguk, we two) and drops pronouns because the verb shows the person — but it has no gender.
